preference_rationale:
I actually like B, but the experiment as set up is infeasible for a nontechnical team. You cannot do a 40,000 firm-quarter panel in Excel, and this firm would not be interested in that kind of analysis even if it is stronger statistically. A is much more fundamentals-driven and is what these five people can actually run and defend to an investment committee that distrusts models it cannot inspect.

This is a feasibility call rather than a judgment that A is the better piece of thinking. B asks the more interesting question; it just cannot be asked this way here.
critique_A:
My chief complaint is that it circumvents the main question - whether the language is actually informative - and just sizes the potential impact instead. It asserts that a CFO sounds the same either way rather than establishing it.

I would also assume the team has already established that this company is sensitive to its vendors' pricing, which is precisely the work A describes. Much of the plan therefore delivers back what the analyst already holds, rather than addressing the new question the call raised.

A treats the vendor's uplift distribution as observable across five to ten comparable customers renewed in the last 24 months. Those deals are private. Gartner, Forrester and SAM benchmarks give directional ranges, not per-customer realized uplift, so the distribution the likelihood weighting rests on is largely unobtainable.

The materiality cuts - under 25bp makes tone moot, over 75bp forces a call - are asserted rather than derived.
critique_B:
The experiment as set up is infeasible for a nontechnical team. A 40,000 firm-quarter panel with embedding-based topic tagging, a pinned LLM, 1,000 hand-labels, elastic-net weighting and block bootstrap cannot be run by five people with no engineers and nobody maintaining a database, and the investment committee is skeptical of models it cannot inspect. Nor would this firm be interested in that kind of analysis even if it is stronger statistically.

Under this error asymmetry the cost is sharper than inconvenience: spending the only analyst on a research programme while the renegotiation resolves is how the fund gets blindsided on the thing it was worried about.

The idea is right. Separating whether this call is genuinely elevated from whether elevation predicts anything is the correct decomposition, and B is honest that the modal outcome is a null. What it needs is a version scaled to this desk - the same two questions asked of this company's own transcript history rather than a market-wide panel.
why_loser_was_defensible: B asks the question the seed actually raises - whether the defensive language carries information - and decomposes it correctly into a measurement claim and a predictive one. An analyst at a firm with the technical capacity to run it would take B and would be right to.
